title: Children and loss
hookLine: Kisa Gotami's story, for parents who have lost a child, told gently
tomorrow: an old fridge-magnet verse about friends. does Buddhism have one?

cards: A gentle word first: today's story is about a child who dies. If that is your story too, take this slowly, or save it for another day.
People who grieve often say the hardest part is what others say: everything happens for a reason, at least you can try again. A young mother named Kisa Gotami heard her own version.
Her little boy died, and she couldn't accept it. She carried him on her hip from house to house, asking everyone for medicine. People shook their heads.
One of them, kinder than the rest, said: go and ask the Buddha.

teach.b: The story comes from the old commentaries, and her own verses are kept in the Therigatha, the songs of the early nuns. She reaches the Buddha and asks for medicine. He doesn't argue.
He doesn't tell her to stop crying.

teach.h: FROM A HOUSE WITH NO DEATH.
teach.b: He says yes: bring me a mustard seed, from a house where no one has died. So she goes door to door again, and this time something changes. Every family has a seed to give, and none can give it.
A father was lost here. A daughter there. A husband.
A grandmother, a baby brother. By evening she understands that her grief is not a strange, lonely thing. It lives in every house on the street.
She lays her son down, gently, and goes back. The story is often told as a hard lesson: everyone dies, so let go. Read slowly, it's softer than that.
The Buddha didn't send her away with an answer.
He sent her to her neighbors, and at every door someone held her loss next to their own. Nobody hurried her. Nobody fixed it.
For a parent who has lost a child, the tradition doesn't offer a reason.

how: Buddhists tell Kisa Gotami's story at funerals and in teaching on grief; families often hold memorial rites with monks or teachers and dedicate merit to the one who died.

o: a debt from a past life that the parent now repays
grief over a child, held by people who have also lost
a test of faith that a parent must pass alone

games.q: Kisa Gotami's road — tap the pairs.
p: a young mother whose son died
a mustard seed from a deathless house
a seed to give, and a loss of its own
the songs of the early nuns

s: in the story, the Buddha tells Kisa Gotami to stop crying and accept death
he doesn't argue with her; he sends her to her neighbors with a request.
the mustard seed story comes from the commentaries; her verses are in the Therigatha
the story is told in the old commentaries, and her own verses are kept with the early nuns'.

games.q: a coworker's sister lost her baby. at lunch the coworker says she has no idea what to text her sister. what does Kisa Gotami's story suggest?
o: send something like: i'm here, no need to answer. then keep showing up.
share the story's lesson: everyone dies, so in time she'll have to let go.
wait until she's doing better, so the text doesn't stir up the grief.
games.why: the Buddha didn't hand her a lesson; he sent her to people who stood with her. company first, no reasons.

practice: Bring to mind parents who have lost a child: people you know, or people you'll never meet. Hold them the way the village held Kisa Gotami, without fixing anything, and silently offer: may you be held gently.
If this loss is your own, let the wish turn toward you, and stay with it as long as you like.

wordCard.voice: Children and loss: Kisa Gotami's road from door to door, where grief turns out to live in every house.

orig.note: Pali: compassion, the wish that someone's suffering be eased.

carryVoice: A line to keep: held gently, by people who have lost too. Eleven of eleven; the family days are done.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary (on verse 114) and Therigatha commentary: the story of Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed
